blocks.title: Hidden routes in first-passage time
blocks.spoken_text: This line of work asks one question: if a random walker can reach the same target by more than one kind of route, what can the full distribution of arrival times tell us about those routes? The shape I care about is an early peak, a valley and a delayed peak. I start from a ring with one target and one directed shortcut, move to two-dimensional lattices, and finish with what changes when there is more than one target.
blocks.timing_prompt: Roadmap: ring, then 2D lattices, then several targets.

blocks.title: What is first-passage time?
blocks.spoken_text: First the quantity. A random walk moves one step at a time at random. The first-passage time is the step at which the walker reaches the target for the first time; the walk stops there. Repeating the walk many times gives a histogram, and in the limit the distribution f(t). An average time would hide its shape: one dominant route usually gives one peak, while two kinds of route with different delays can leave two peaks.
blocks.timing_prompt: The animation shows the walk stopping at the target and the histogram building up.

blocks.title: Why a double peak matters
blocks.spoken_text: This is why the shape matters. A single peak usually means one dominant arrival timescale. A double peak often signals two groups of paths with different delays, and the valley between them is the time range where neither group dominates. The shape is a clue to the mechanism, not a proof: each case still has to be checked, which is what the next slides do.

blocks.title: One ring, one shortcut: one sharp case and one split case
blocks.spoken_text: The simplest computed example: a ring of 100 sites, one absorbing target, and one directed shortcut from site 6 to the site just beyond the target. Everywhere else the walker stays, steps left or steps right with probability one third each. Only the rule at the shortcut site changes between the two panels. If the shortcut is taken with probability one quarter, most walkers use it quickly: one sharp peak at step 27 and a long tail. If it is taken rarely, the distribution splits: an early peak at step 51 made almost entirely of walkers that used the shortcut, and a late peak near step 1,021 where three quarters of the walkers never used it. So a shortcut does not automatically give two peaks; two peaks appear when the two kinds of route are separated in time and both carry weight.
blocks.timing_prompt: Both panels are exact computations; the y-axes differ.

blocks.title: Where the shortcut lands decides whether a second peak appears
blocks.spoken_text: Next, a second ring model, in which each step can go up to three sites either way and the shortcut leaves from the start. Here I move the shortcut's landing site around the ring. Only a few landing sites, 36 to 39 and 62 to 64, give a second peak that is well separated from the first, around step 100. When the shortcut lands right next to the target, the two maxima are only two to four steps apart, which is too close to read as two kinds of route. For most landing sites there is no second peak at all. So where the route goes matters, and not monotonically.
blocks.timing_prompt: This is a different ring model from the previous slide.

blocks.title: Two 2D layouts that keep two timescales visible
blocks.spoken_text: In two dimensions, the layout decides whether two timescales survive. Two layouts that do: a corridor whose walls occasionally let the walker through, with one target at the far end; and an open lattice with one target near the start and one far away. Both computed distributions have two clear peaks by the report's classifier. In the corridor, the competition is between going straight along the corridor and spending time outside it; with two targets, target competition is added.
blocks.timing_prompt: Both curves are exact computations; the small layout drawings are schematic.

blocks.title: Time outside the corridor, or crossing its wall?
blocks.spoken_text: For a one-target corridor, is the late peak mainly about time spent outside the corridor, or about crossing the wall itself? Comparing hits in the valley with hits in the late window: late hits spend far more steps outside the corridor before reaching the target, about 1,300 against 700 when the walls are closed or nearly closed, while the probability of having crossed a wall is almost the same in both windows. So, in this set-up, wall crossing matters, but the delay comes mainly from the time spent outside.
blocks.timing_prompt: Values are as published in the corridor report, which gives no uncertainty.

blocks.title: From two targets to many
blocks.spoken_text: With two targets a peak can belong to a particular target. In the open-lattice case, the early window is entirely near-target hits and the late window almost entirely far-target hits. With many possible targets, new questions appear: nearby targets can screen far ones, groups of targets can compete, and a few walkers may reach a distant target very late. The open question is which mechanism makes the distribution bimodal when route competition and target competition act together.
blocks.timing_prompt: Ends the physics with the open question.

blocks.title: Minimal mathematical backbone
blocks.spoken_text: Behind every figure is the same small set of objects. Probability moves over the sites by a discrete-time master equation, including the chance of staying put, and mass that reaches the target is removed because the target is absorbing. T is the first step at which the walker is on the target. The survival probability S(t) is the chance that this has not happened by step t, and the first-passage distribution f(t) is what S loses at step t.
blocks.timing_prompt: A compact anchor, not a derivation.
